analysis.one_liner: Makes the individual income tax cuts from the 2017 tax law permanent instead of letting them expire after 2025.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2018 with no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 Republican tax law cut individual income tax rates for everyone, but to keep the law's official cost down, those rate cuts were written to expire at the end of 2025 and revert to higher rates. This bill, from Senator Ted Cruz, would delete that expiration date and make the lower rates permanent — including the new 37% top rate on income above $600,000 for married couples, the new capital gains brackets, and the law's changes to how children's investment income is taxed. The bill never got a hearing in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, every household paying income tax would keep the lower 2017-law rates past 2025 — middle-income families would keep the 12% and 22% brackets, for example. But the largest dollar gains would go to the highest earners: the 37% top rate on income above $600,000 for joint filers would become permanent, as would the new capital gains brackets and the rewritten rules taxing children's investment income. Because the 2017 rate structure delivers proportionally the biggest cuts at the top, making it permanent is worth the most to the wealthiest households, with the lost revenue adding to deficits that eventually must be paid for.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, then taxpayers at all incomes

how_it_helps.text: The individual income tax rates created by the 2017 tax law — 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, and 37% — would no longer expire after 2025, keeping taxes lower for households at every income level than they would otherwise be.

The bill would permanently extend the 37% top rate on income above $600,000 for joint filers (about $500,000 for singles), and permanently extend the new capital gains brackets that tax long-term gains at 0% up to $77,200 of taxable income for joint filers and 15% up to $479,000, with the 20% rate only above that.
It would permanently rewrite the 'kiddie tax' rules so that a child's unearned income is taxed under the estate-and-trust rate tables rather than at the parents' rate, as the 2017 law provided.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — and ultimately taxpayers — would bear the cost. Making the individual rate cuts permanent would add hundreds of billions of dollars to deficits over the next decade, because the scheduled 2025 expiration was the mechanism that kept the 2017 law's official ten-year price tag within budget rules. If future Congresses respond with spending cuts, ordinary people who rely on government programs would share that burden.

drawbacks.text: The individual rates in the 2017 tax law were scheduled to expire at the end of 2025 — that expiration was how the law was made to fit within budget rules limiting its official cost. Making the rates permanent would add hundreds of billions of dollars to federal deficits over a decade, increasing pressure for future spending cuts or tax increases elsewhere.

The bill would also permanently rewrite how children's investment income is taxed, applying the special estate-and-trust rate brackets to kids' unearned income — a change whose largest benefits flow to higher-income families with investment income held in a child's name, not to typical wage-earning households.

By resetting the inflation-indexing baseline to 2018 in the rate tables, the bill locks in the 2017 law's slower inflation adjustment (the chained CPI) for future years, which over time pushes taxpayers into higher brackets faster than the old method did.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real for taxpayers at every income level, who would keep the lower rates they received under the 2017 law beyond 2025. The cost is that the largest dollar gains go to the top bracket and to families able to shift investment income to children, and that permanence would add several hundred billion dollars to deficits over a decade because the 2025 expiration was the mechanism that limited the 2017 law's official price tag. A more balanced design might have made the cuts permanent only for middle- and lower-income brackets while letting the top rate revert, paying for the difference; this bill does neither.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 10, 2018.
On the same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No further action was ever taken: the Finance Committee never considered it and the full Senate never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, leaving Cruz as the bill's only supporter in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthier households are better off than they would have been had the bill passed, because the tax cuts at the top of the income scale and the favorable kiddie-tax rules still expire after 2025 as scheduled. Everyday taxpayers are unaffected so far, since the current rates remain in place until their scheduled 2025 sunset either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Deficit-conscious status quo; top-rate cuts still expire

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2017 tax law's individual rates permanent; no other senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the remainder of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party breakdown exists; the bill was introduced by a Republican with zero cosponsors of either party and died in committee without opposition ever having to organize.

industries.note: The top rate on wage income above $600,000 (joint) would drop permanently from 39.6% to 37%, and the new capital gains brackets — with the 20% rate not starting until roughly $479,000 of taxable income for joint filers — would also become permanent. Because the largest dollar savings under the 2017 rate structure go to the highest earners, permanence is worth the most to them.

industries.industry: Wealthy families with investment income in children's names
industries.note: The permanent kiddie-tax rewrite taxes a child's unearned income under the low-bracket estate-and-trust tables, a change mainly valuable to families shifting investment income to children; ordinary wage-earning families with little or no investment income for their kids see little from it.

They would keep the lower 10%–24% brackets past 2025, a genuine and visible benefit on a paycheck. But because the bill packages this together with permanent cuts at the very top and no offsetting revenue, the middle-class benefit cannot be separated from the transfer to wealthier households — and the added deficits eventually fall back on everyone.
